```{r co-occurrence-values}
# medians of each study and group
study_medians <- cooc_median |>
  filter(column != columns[1]) |>
  select(-significant) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = r)
study_tests <- filter(cooc_tests, column != columns[1])
n_significant <- \(g, tp) sum(study_tests$p[study_tests$group == g & study_tests$type == tp] < 0.05)
hmp_test <- \(tp, field) filter(cooc_tests, column == columns[1], type == tp)[[field]]
ctest <- \(g, tp, field) filter(combined_tests, group == g, type == tp)[[field]]
n_studies <- \(pt, cmp) with(filter(study_medians, pair == pt), sum(cmp(Periodontitis, Health)))
med_range <- \(pt, g) sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(study_medians[[g]][study_medians$pair == pt]),
                              max(study_medians[[g]][study_medians$pair == pt]))
hc <- \(a, b) sprintf("%.2f", hmp_cor[a, b])
pm <- \(type, src = "healthy") sprintf("%.2f", median(pair_cor_participants[[src]][pair_cor_participants$pair == type],
                                                     na.rm = TRUE))
pc <- \(x, y, src) sprintf("%.2f", pair_cor_participants[[src]][pair_cor_participants$a == x & pair_cor_participants$b == y])
neg_pairs <- filter(pair_cor, healthy < 0)
n_neg <- \(type) sum(neg_pairs$pair == type)
n_neg_with <- \(type, genera) with(filter(neg_pairs, pair == type), sum(a %in% genera | b %in% genera))
# the same correlations on relative abundance instead of CLR, for comparison
pm_relative <- \(g) pair_cor |>
  inner_join(combined_cor(g, participant_genera, "abundance"), by = c("a", "b")) |>
  filter(pair == "Both increased") |>
  with(sprintf("%.2f", median(r)))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Figure details
**HMP panel**

- **Each point**: one pair of genera, plotted at its Spearman correlation of CLR abundance across the 183 HMP healthy subgingival plaque samples (16S V3–V5, first visit). CLR: log of the genus's reads minus the mean log reads of all genera detected in subgingival plaque, in the same sample; zeros replaced by half the sample's smallest count.
- **Genera**: the 20 + 20 top periodontitis genera from the genus heatmaps, kept if they reach ≥0.1% abundance in ≥10% of samples *and* exist under that name in HMP. That leaves 27 genera: 13 increased (*Tannerella*, *Treponema*, *Porphyromonas*, *Prevotella*, *Filifactor*, *Peptostreptococcus*, *Fusobacterium*, *Selenomonas*, *Dialister*, *Campylobacter*, *Anaeroglobus*, *Johnsonella*, *Aggregatibacter*) and 14 decreased. Missing: e.g. *Desulfobulbus*, *Fretibacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Mogibacterium*, *Alloprevotella*, *Schaalia*; *Cutibacterium* is present under its old name *Propionibacterium*.
- **Pairs**: 351 = 78 both increased + 91 both decreased + 182 one of each. Bar = median of the row.
- **Test statistics**: median correlation of the both-increased pairs (`r pm("Both increased")`) − median of the opposite-way pairs (`r pm("One increased,\none decreased")`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", hmp_test("increased", "gap"))`; the same for the both-decreased pairs (`r pm("Both decreased")`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", hmp_test("decreased", "gap"))`. Two separate tests, so that one pair type cannot carry the other.
- **Null**: the 13 increased / 14 decreased labels are shuffled among the 27 genera 1,000 times and each statistic is recomputed (97.5th percentile `r sprintf("%.2f", hmp_test("increased", "null_975"))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", hmp_test("decreased", "null_975"))`). One-sided p = (1 + number ≥ observed) ÷ 1,001 = `r signif(hmp_test("increased", "p"), 2)` and `r signif(hmp_test("decreased", "p"), 2)`.
- **Example**: *Treponema*–*Tannerella* = `r hc("Treponema", "Tannerella")` (both increased, positive); *Tannerella*–*Rothia* = `r hc("Tannerella", "Rothia")` (opposite, negative).
- **Exceptions**: `r n_neg("Both increased")` of 78 both-increased pairs are negative, `r n_neg_with("Both increased", c("Filifactor", "Campylobacter", "Johnsonella"))` of them involving *Filifactor*, *Campylobacter* or *Johnsonella*. `r n_neg("Both decreased")` of 91 both-decreased pairs are negative, `r n_neg_with("Both decreased", "Oribacterium")` of them involving *Oribacterium*, which is decreased in only `r perio_genera$decreased[perio_genera$taxon == "Oribacterium"]` of `r perio_genera$signatures[perio_genera$taxon == "Oribacterium"]` periodontitis signatures (e.g. *Neisseria*–*Oribacterium* `r hc("Neisseria", "Oribacterium")`).
- **Watch out**: CLR removes most of the effect of relative abundances summing to one, but it is not absolute abundance: a shift of the whole community still changes it. On relative abundance instead, the same-side vs opposite-side difference holds, but pairs of increased genera look more correlated in health (median `r pm_relative("Health")` in the healthy participants of the five studies, against `r pm("Both increased", "health_studies")` on CLR), mostly because when the dominant decreased genera (e.g. *Streptococcus*) take a larger share, the shares of all minor genera fall together. The direction labels come from PerioSigDB reporting, not from HMP.

**Study columns**

- **Participants:** untreated periodontitis 62 (Studies 1141 13, 1411 18, 191 15, 428 7, 484 9) and healthy 51 (11, 13, 13, 7, 7); subgingival plaque only, each participant's samples averaged. Studies 484 and 428 sampled several sites per participant.
- **Genera:** the same 27 genera; all are found in the five studies (HOMD taxonomy; *Cutibacterium* matched to HMP's *Propionibacterium*). CLR over each participant's full genus profile (genus reads ÷ all reads after quality filtering, averaged over the participant's samples), zeros replaced by half the participant's smallest non-zero value. A genus never detected in a study's group gives no correlation there.
- **Within-study correlations:** computed separately in each study, so that differences in 16S region, platform and depth between studies do not create correlations. Each pair has a correlation in all 5 studies. With 7–18 participants per study and group, a single study's correlations are noisy.
- **Combined across studies:** for the tests in the title and the medians in the text, each pair's correlations in the five studies are combined by the mean of Fisher's z weighted by participants − 3, separately for health and periodontitis (correlations clipped to ±0.99 before Fisher's z).
- **Pair medians, combined (HMP health / study health / periodontitis):** both increased `r pm("Both increased")` / `r pm("Both increased", "health_studies")` / `r pm("Both increased", "periodontitis")`; both decreased `r pm("Both decreased")` / `r pm("Both decreased", "health_studies")` / `r pm("Both decreased", "periodontitis")`; one of each `r pm("One increased,\none decreased")` / `r pm("One increased,\none decreased", "health_studies")` / `r pm("One increased,\none decreased", "periodontitis")`.
- **Tests:** the two tests of the HMP panel, within each study and group (p in the figure) and on the combined correlations (title). Combined, periodontitis: both increased minus opposite-way `r sprintf("%.2f", ctest("Periodontitis", "increased", "gap"))` (p = `r signif(ctest("Periodontitis", "increased", "p"), 2)`), both decreased minus opposite-way `r sprintf("%.2f", ctest("Periodontitis", "decreased", "gap"))` (p = `r signif(ctest("Periodontitis", "decreased", "p"), 2)`); health `r sprintf("%.2f", ctest("Health", "increased", "gap"))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", ctest("Health", "decreased", "gap"))`.
- **Example:** *Tannerella*–*Treponema* `r hc("Tannerella", "Treponema")` in HMP health, `r pc("Tannerella", "Treponema", "health_studies")` in study health, `r pc("Tannerella", "Treponema", "periodontitis")` in periodontitis; *Rothia*–*Tannerella* `r hc("Rothia", "Tannerella")`, `r pc("Rothia", "Tannerella", "health_studies")` and `r pc("Rothia", "Tannerella", "periodontitis")`.
- **Agreement of the two healthy sources:** Spearman, combined `r sprintf("%.2f", with(pair_cor_participants, cor(healthy, health_studies, method = "spearman")))` across pairs between HMP and the healthy participants of the five studies, so the study data reproduce the HMP pattern.
- **Watch out:** 7–18 participants per study and group, so each pair's correlation is imprecise; the pattern across many pairs is more reliable than any single pair. Pairs share genera, so pairs are not independent.
:::

**Shows:** in healthy plaque, genera that change the same way in periodontitis also tend to rise and fall together. Pairs of periodontitis-decreased genera are mostly positively correlated (median `r pm("Both decreased")`), and so, more weakly, are pairs of periodontitis-increased genera (median `r pm("Both increased")`); both are more correlated than pairs that change in opposite ways (p = `r signif(hmp_test("decreased", "p"), 2)` and `r signif(hmp_test("increased", "p"), 2)`), and so are both in the healthy participants of most of the five studies (increased: `r n_significant("Health", "increased")` of 5 studies, decreased: `r n_significant("Health", "decreased")` of 5); *Treponema* and *Tannerella*, for example, are positively correlated across healthy participants (`r hc("Treponema", "Tannerella")`). A periodontitis-increased and a periodontitis-decreased genus are mostly negatively correlated (median `r pm("One increased,\none decreased")`): participants with relatively more *Tannerella* tend to have relatively less *Rothia* (`r hc("Tannerella", "Rothia")`). This is consistent with some disease-associated groupings being present within healthy-community variation, but these are cross-sectional healthy samples only: they do not establish a trajectory from health to periodontitis or direct ecological interactions. Most of the negatively correlated pairs of periodontitis-decreased genera involve *Oribacterium*, which is only weakly supported as decreased in periodontitis (`r perio_genera$decreased[perio_genera$taxon == "Oribacterium"]` of `r perio_genera$signatures[perio_genera$taxon == "Oribacterium"]` signatures) and in healthy plaque correlates with the periodontitis-increased genera. Most of the negatively correlated pairs of periodontitis-increased genera involve *Filifactor*, *Campylobacter* or *Johnsonella*. The Human Microbiome Project screened its participants for oral health, so this variation exists without diagnosed periodontitis, though it may include mild gingival inflammation.

**Shows:** across individual patients with periodontitis (the 62 in the five studies with per-sample data), pairs of periodontitis-decreased genera are still more correlated than pairs that change in opposite ways (combined p = `r signif(ctest("Periodontitis", "decreased", "p"), 2)`; significant within `r n_significant("Periodontitis", "decreased")` of the 5 studies), but pairs of periodontitis-increased genera only weakly so (combined p = `r signif(ctest("Periodontitis", "increased", "p"), 2)`; significant within `r n_significant("Periodontitis", "increased")` of 5 studies, against `r n_significant("Health", "increased")` of 5 in their healthy participants). Pairs of increased genera have a lower median in periodontitis than in health in `r n_studies("Both increased", \(p, h) p < h)` of the 5 studies (combined across studies, `r pm("Both increased", "periodontitis")` against `r pm("Both increased", "health_studies")`, and `r pm("Both increased")` in HMP), though in health the study medians range from `r med_range("Both increased", "Health")` and are highest in Study 484, which has only 7 healthy participants. Pairs of an increased and a decreased genus are negative in health in `r n_studies("One increased,\none decreased", \(p, h) h < 0)` of 5 studies and closer to 0 in periodontitis in `r n_studies("One increased,\none decreased", \(p, h) abs(p) < abs(h))` (*Rothia*–*Tannerella*, combined: `r pc("Rothia", "Tannerella", "health_studies")` in health, `r pc("Rothia", "Tannerella", "periodontitis")` in periodontitis). The pairs of periodontitis-decreased genera keep their correlations overall (combined median `r pm("Both decreased", "periodontitis")`, against `r pm("Both decreased", "health_studies")` in health), but their study medians in periodontitis vary widely (`r med_range("Both decreased", "Periodontitis")`). One reading is that, in health, participants differ along a gradient from more to less periodontitis-like plaque, which makes the increased genera rise together and the decreased genera fall; in periodontitis that gradient is weaker or absent. The next figure tests one alternative, that the increased genera simply vary less between patients. This is cross-sectional and the periodontitis groups are small, so it describes co-variation within each group, not how communities change as disease develops.

```{r genus-spread}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-cap: "Each genus of the figure above in the healthy participants (x) and periodontitis patients (y) of the five studies: share of participants with the genus (left), median relative abundance (middle) and spread of relative abundance across the participants who have the genus (right: standard deviation of log10 relative abundance). Computed within each study and averaged across studies, weighted by participants. Colors: direction in periodontitis (PerioSigDB). Dashed line: equal in both groups."
# spread only among participants with the genus, so that it does not repeat the share with the genus;
# studies with fewer than 3 such participants are left out
present_spread <- participant_genera |>
  filter(abundance > 0) |>
  summarise(spread = sd(log10(abundance)), n = n(), .by = c(Study, group, taxon)) |>
  filter(n >= 3) |>
  summarise(spread = weighted.mean(spread, n), .by = c(group, taxon))
genus_stats <- participant_genera |>
  summarise(prevalence = mean(abundance > 0), median = median(abundance), n = n(), .by = c(Study, group, taxon)) |>
  summarise(across(c(prevalence, median), \(x) weighted.mean(x, n)), .by = c(group, taxon)) |>
  left_join(present_spread, by = c("group", "taxon")) |>
  pivot_longer(c(prevalence, median, spread), names_to = "stat") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(direction = str_to_sentence(perio_dir[taxon]))

stat_labels <- c(prevalence = "Participants with the genus", median = "Median relative abundance (%)",
                 spread = "Spread when present: SD of log10 relative abundance")
genus_stats |>
  mutate(across(c(Health, Periodontitis), \(x) ifelse(stat == "median", 100 * x, x)),
         stat = factor(stat_labels[stat], levels = stat_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Health, Periodontitis, fill = direction)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.4, color = "grey15", stroke = 0.3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = taxon, color = direction), size = 2.6, fontface = "italic", seed = 1,
                  max.overlaps = 8, segment.color = "grey70", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Increased = "#c2410c", Decreased = "#1c5cab"), name = "In periodontitis") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Increased = "#c2410c", Decreased = "#1c5cab")) +
  facet_wrap(~stat, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Healthy participants", y = "Periodontitis patients")
```

```{r genus-spread-values}
gs <- \(st, dir, grp, pct = FALSE) {
  v <- median(genus_stats[[grp]][genus_stats$stat == st & genus_stats$direction == dir])
  if (pct) scales::percent(v, if (st == "median") 0.1 else 1) else sprintf("%.2f", v)
}
# correlation each pair of increased genera would have in periodontitis if it kept its correlation in the
# healthy participants and only the spread of the two genera changed (attenuation by a narrower range:
# r k / sqrt(1 - r^2 + r^2 k^2), k = spread in periodontitis / spread in health, geometric mean of the two)
spread_ratio <- present_spread |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = spread) |>
  with(setNames(Periodontitis / Health, taxon))
attenuation <- pair_cor_participants |>
  filter(pair == "Both increased", !is.na(periodontitis), !is.na(health_studies)) |>
  mutate(k = sqrt(spread_ratio[a] * spread_ratio[b]),
         expected = health_studies * k / sqrt(1 - health_studies^2 + health_studies^2 * k^2))
att <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f", median(x))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Figure details
- **Each point:** one of the 27 genera of the figures above (*Propionibacterium* is *Cutibacterium*, under HMP's name). Participants and relative abundance as in the figure above.
- **Within study, then combined:** each statistic is computed in each study and group, then averaged across the five studies weighted by participants, so differences in 16S region between studies do not enter.
- **Spread:** standard deviation of log10 relative abundance across the participants who have the genus (studies with at least 3 of them); participants without the genus are left out, so spread measures how much the amount varies, not how often the genus is missing (that is the left panel).
- **Expected correlation:** for each pair of increased genera, the correlation in the healthy participants of the five studies (r) shrunk by the change in spread, r k / sqrt(1 − r² + r²k²), where k is the ratio of spread in periodontitis to spread in health (geometric mean of the two genera). This is how much a correlation weakens when the range of the data narrows and nothing else changes.
- **Medians over genera (health → periodontitis):** increased genera: participants with the genus `r gs("prevalence", "Increased", "Health", TRUE)` → `r gs("prevalence", "Increased", "Periodontitis", TRUE)`, median relative abundance `r gs("median", "Increased", "Health", TRUE)` → `r gs("median", "Increased", "Periodontitis", TRUE)`, spread `r gs("spread", "Increased", "Health")` → `r gs("spread", "Increased", "Periodontitis")`. Decreased genera: `r gs("prevalence", "Decreased", "Health", TRUE)` → `r gs("prevalence", "Decreased", "Periodontitis", TRUE)`, `r gs("median", "Decreased", "Health", TRUE)` → `r gs("median", "Decreased", "Periodontitis", TRUE)`, spread `r gs("spread", "Decreased", "Health")` → `r gs("spread", "Decreased", "Periodontitis")`.
- **No test:** descriptive; 7–18 participants per study and group.
:::

**Shows:** the genera increased in periodontitis are found in more patients than healthy participants and at higher abundance, and in the patients who have them most vary less in amount (median spread `r gs("spread", "Increased", "Health")` → `r gs("spread", "Increased", "Periodontitis")`; e.g. *Johnsonella*, *Prevotella*, *Anaeroglobus*, *Treponema*, *Fusobacterium*, *Selenomonas*). *Peptostreptococcus* and *Filifactor* are the exceptions, with a wider spread. The decreased genera are less often found and less abundant in periodontitis, and their spread is about unchanged (`r gs("spread", "Decreased", "Health")` → `r gs("spread", "Decreased", "Periodontitis")`). The narrower spread does not explain the weaker correlations of the increased genera in the figure above: on its own it would lower their median correlation from `r att(attenuation$health_studies)` to `r att(attenuation$expected)`, against `r att(attenuation$periodontitis)` observed. Most of the weakening is therefore not explained by spread.


### Agreement across approaches

```{r method-agreement}
# conditions passing FDR < 0.05 in the same direction as periodontitis, by approach
fdr_hits <- \(d) paste(sort(unique(d$Condition)), collapse = ", ")
method_agreement <- tribble(
  ~Approach, ~`Compared with`, ~Conditions,
  "Genus enrichment", "all BugSigDB studies",
  fdr_hits(filter(bind_rows(enrichment_table("increased"), enrichment_table("decreased")), fdr < 0.05)),
  "Genus enrichment", "same body site group",
  fdr_hits(filter(bind_rows(enrichment_table("increased", match_site = TRUE),
                            enrichment_table("decreased", match_site = TRUE)), fdr < 0.05)),
  "Genus direction", "50% (no direction preference)",
  fdr_hits(filter(bind_rows(direction_tests("increased"), direction_tests("decreased")), fdr < 0.05, same / n > 0.5)),
  "Whole-signature similarity", "all BugSigDB study units",
  fdr_hits(filter(semsim_tests$stats, kind == "all", fdr < 0.05, perio == direction)),
  "Whole-signature similarity", "same body site group",
  fdr_hits(filter(semsim_tests$stats, kind == "site", fdr < 0.05, perio == direction)),
  "Jaccard genus overlap", "all BugSigDB study units",
  fdr_hits(filter(jaccard_tests$all, fdr < 0.05, perio == direction)),
  "Jaccard genus overlap", "same body site group",
  fdr_hits(filter(jaccard_tests$site, fdr < 0.05, perio == direction))
)
kbl(method_agreement, caption = "Conditions significantly similar to periodontitis (FDR < 0.05, same direction as periodontitis) in each literature-based approach.") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Table details
- **What a row lists**: conditions with at least one FDR < 0.05 result in the same direction as periodontitis in that approach. For genus approaches, that means any of the 20 top genera in that direction.
- **Genus enrichment, all studies**: one-sided Fisher's exact test of the share of the condition's study units with the genus vs all other units of that direction (conditions with ≥5 units). BH across all genus × condition tests per direction.
- **Genus enrichment, same body site group**: the same test, but one-sided exact Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel stratified by body site group.
- **Genus direction**: two-sided binomial test of a condition's units reporting the genus increased vs decreased; listed only if FDR < 0.05 and the majority is in the periodontitis direction.
- **Whole-signature similarity / Jaccard**: one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test of the condition's study-unit similarities against those of all other conditions of that direction, with BH within each column. "Same body site group": the condition's units from one site group against other conditions' units from that site group (gut, mouth or urogenital, which have enough other conditions). Jaccard compares genera only, with the consensus taxa mapped to genus.
- **Reading**: only colorectal cancer survives all seven. The four other conditions listed without site matching (COVID-19, head and neck cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, smoking) all drop out once compared within the same body site group, except rheumatoid arthritis mouth studies in Jaccard overlap (increased signatures, FDR 0.04).
:::

Colorectal cancer is the only condition every approach flags, and the only one whose overlap survives BH correction in the body-site-stratified genus enrichment and in both taxonomic-similarity measures. Four genera carry it: colorectal cancer studies report *Fusobacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus* and *Porphyromonas* increased far more often than other conditions sampled at the same sites, and whole-signature similarity finds the same overlap with taxa kept at their reported ranks. Every other condition depends on the method: several oral conditions pass before body site stratification and none after it.

The same four genera are higher in cancer in participant-level stool data, so the overlap is not an artefact of what gets published. The periodontitis-decreased signature shows nothing equivalent in either the literature or the stool datasets.

```{r bsdb-robustness}
# is colorectal cancer singled out because it is one of the largest conditions?
set.seed(1)
inc_sigs <- filter(bsdb_sigs, direction == "increased")
core <- c("Fusobacterium", "Parvimonas", "Peptostreptococcus", "Porphyromonas")
core_hits <- bsdb_genera |> filter(direction == "increased", taxon %in% core) |> distinct(sig, taxon)
large <- inc_sigs |> count(Condition, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 4)
large_oe <- site_expected(inc_sigs, core_hits) |>
  filter(Condition %in% large$Condition) |>
  summarise(max_ratio = max(observed / expected), .by = Condition)
# similarity of their gut study units to the periodontitis-increased consensus, vs other conditions' gut units
large_sim <- semsim_tests$stats |> filter(kind == "site", site == "gastrointestinal", direction == "increased",
                                          perio == "increased", Condition %in% large$Condition)
others <- setdiff(large$Condition, "Colorectal cancer")
others_sim <- paste(sprintf("%s %.2f", others, large_sim$mean_rank[match(others, large_sim$Condition)]), collapse = ", ")

# subsample colorectal cancer to 15 study units
crc_sigs <- filter(inc_sigs, Condition == "Colorectal cancer")
sub_enrich <- replicate(200, {
  keep <- sample(crc_sigs$sig, 15)
  s2 <- filter(inc_sigs, Condition != "Colorectal cancer" | sig %in% keep)
  sapply(core, \(g) site_matched_p("Colorectal cancer", g, s2, core_hits)) < 0.05
})
gut_inc <- filter(semsim_scores, direction == "increased", perio == "increased", site_group == "gastrointestinal")
crc_sim <- gut_inc$sim[gut_inc$Condition == "Colorectal cancer"]
other_sim <- gut_inc$sim[gut_inc$Condition != "Colorectal cancer"]
sub_sim <- replicate(1000, wilcox.test(sample(crc_sim, 15), other_sim, alternative = "greater", exact = FALSE)$p.value < 0.05)
pct <- \(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Robustness details
- **Largest conditions**: by number of increased study units: Parkinson's disease 59, colorectal cancer 54, COVID-19 42, obesity 39.
- **Observed ÷ expected**: share of the condition's units reporting each of *Fusobacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus* and *Porphyromonas* increased ÷ the share in other conditions from the same body site groups, weighted by the condition's site mix. Colorectal cancer: up to 13.3× (e.g. *Parvimonas* 0.41 vs 0.03 expected). The other three: at most 1.09×.
- **Similarity ranks** (gut study units' increased signatures vs the periodontitis-increased consensus, compared with other conditions' gut units; 0.5 = typical): `r paste(sprintf("%s %.2f (FDR %s)", large_sim$Condition, large_sim$mean_rank, signif(large_sim$fdr, 1)), collapse = ", ")`.
- **Subsampling enrichment**: 200 draws of 15 of colorectal cancer's 54 increased units. Each genus is re-tested with the one-sided site-stratified exact test, unadjusted p < 0.05. Significant in 97% (*Porphyromonas*) to 100% (*Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus*) of draws.
- **Subsampling similarity**: 1,000 draws of 15 of its `r length(crc_sim)` gut units, one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test against the `r length(other_sim)` gut units of other conditions, p < 0.05 in `r pct(mean(sub_sim))` of draws.
- **Watch out**: subsampling keeps the other conditions fixed and uses unadjusted p, so it shows the signal is not just a sample-size effect, not that it would pass FDR at n = 15.
:::

**Robustness:** colorectal cancer is not singled out simply because it is one of the largest conditions in BugSigDB. The other largest conditions (`r paste(others, collapse = ", ")`) show none of the signal: none reports any of *Fusobacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus* or *Porphyromonas* more than `r sprintf("%.1f", max(large_oe$max_ratio[large_oe$Condition != "Colorectal cancer"]))` times as often as expected, and their similarity ranks to the periodontitis-increased signature are `r others_sim` (0.5 = typical). When colorectal cancer is cut to 15 random study units, the size of a typical condition, the four genera stay significantly enriched in `r pct(min(rowMeans(sub_enrich)))`–`r pct(max(rowMeans(sub_enrich)))` of draws and the similarity in `r pct(mean(sub_sim))`.

# Summary and limitations

PerioSigDB varies in comparison-group definitions, participant characteristics, clinical measurement and profiling method, and its metadata are uneven, worst for systemic health status and the clinical measures. Despite that, its increased signatures agree across studies more than site-matched random sets do, and the agreement holds when the targeted assays are dropped. Colorectal cancer is the one condition whose literature overlaps the periodontitis signature by every approach here, through *Fusobacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus* and *Porphyromonas*, and that overlap reappears in participant-level stool data.

These are associations reported in the published literature. They do not establish a causal relationship between periodontitis and colorectal cancer, bacterial transfer between body sites, or diagnostic value. Limitations:

- **Assay coverage:** about half of PerioSigDB signatures come from targeted assays, so reporting frequencies partly reflect which taxa were measured. Sequencing studies alone recover 18 of the 20 increased and 17 of the 20 decreased genera; *Aggregatibacter* and *Campylobacter* are the exceptions, supported mainly by panel studies.
- **Sampling sites:** body site groups are broad; PerioSigDB is subgingival plaque, while BugSigDB oral studies include saliva, tongue and other sites.
- **Taxonomic resolution:** aggregating species to genus loses specificity. Nine of the 40 genera in the heatmaps contain species reported in both directions (e.g. *P. gingivalis* increased, *P. catoniae* decreased; *S. sanguinis* decreased, *S. anginosus* increased).
- **Metadata:** incomplete, and "not reported" can mean "not entered".
- **Independence:** studies and datasets are treated as independent, although some share cohorts or authors.
- **Comparisons:** the BugSigDB disease-vs-control filter works on group names, and comparison groups in PerioSigDB include some participants with gingivitis and periodontitis-resistant older adults.
